questions.explanation: The sum of roots is -(k-3)=3-k. Set 3-k=5 to get k=-2.

questions.text: Biologist Mina Patel first describes how urban light can disrupt moth navigation. She then presents a study showing that moths exposed to warmer-colored streetlights changed direction less often than moths exposed to blue-rich lights. Which choice best describes the function of the study in the text?
options: It provides evidence relevant to the problem introduced earlier.
It introduces a historical explanation for moth migration.
It challenges the idea that light affects moth behavior at all.
It defines a technical term used by city planners.
questions.explanation: The study supplies evidence about the light-related navigation problem introduced in the first sentence.

questions.text: A passage explains that mangrove roots slow moving water and trap sediment. It then notes that this process can gradually build up shorelines. What is the function of the second sentence?
options: It gives an example unrelated to the first sentence.
It states a consequence of the process described in the first sentence.
questions.explanation: The second sentence explains what can result from roots slowing water and trapping sediment.

questions.text: A text begins by describing a common belief that handwritten notes improve memory. It then states, “However, several recent experiments have found little difference when students review both kinds of notes in the same way.” What is the function of the quoted sentence?
options: It provides a counterpoint to the belief introduced earlier.
It gives a definition of handwritten notes.
It repeats the original belief in stronger terms.
questions.explanation: “However” signals a contrast, and the sentence presents findings that complicate the initial belief.

questions.text: A passage first identifies a decline in bee populations, next lists several possible causes, and finally describes a study designed to test one of those causes. Which choice best describes the overall structure?
options: A phenomenon is introduced, possible explanations are presented, and one explanation is investigated.
Two historical periods are compared before a conclusion is rejected.
A process is described in chronological order without any evaluation.
A claim is stated and then supported only with a definition.
questions.explanation: The sequence is decline -> possible causes -> study of one cause.

questions.text: A text describes how an old bridge was built in 1912, repaired in 1954, widened in 1987, and replaced in 2020. Which structure does the text primarily use?
questions.explanation: The information is organized by time from earliest to latest.

questions.text: Researchers once assumed that a desert plant opened its pores only at night. The text then explains that new sensors detected brief daytime openings after rare rainstorms. The final sentence suggests that the plant may use a more flexible water strategy than previously thought. Which choice best describes the overall structure?
options: A traditional view is presented, new evidence complicates it, and a revised interpretation is proposed.
A process is described, then a completely unrelated example is added.
Two scientists are compared and one is criticized.
A theory is defined and then repeated without evidence.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from prior belief to new evidence to a revised conclusion.

questions.text: A text states that a city planted trees along several hot streets. It then reports lower afternoon surface temperatures on those streets than on similar unplanted streets. The text ends by noting that tree planting alone cannot solve all forms of urban heat. What is the function of the final sentence?
options: It qualifies the significance of the earlier evidence.
It proves the temperature measurements were inaccurate.
It introduces the tree-planting program for the first time.
It explains how surface temperature is measured.
questions.explanation: The final sentence limits the scope of the evidence instead of rejecting it.

questions.text: An author describes a new battery material, explains why its microscopic structure should improve charging speed, and then reports laboratory results consistent with that prediction. Which choice best describes the structure?
options: A claim is introduced, a mechanism is explained, and supporting evidence is presented.
A historical event is narrated and then compared with a modern one.
A problem is introduced but no solution or evidence is discussed.
Several unrelated facts are listed without a central idea.
questions.explanation: The author moves logically from idea to mechanism to test results.

questions.text: A passage states, “The first survey found strong public support for the proposal.” The next sentence begins, “That result, though encouraging to supporters, did not reveal how strongly respondents held their views.” What is the function of the second sentence?
options: It adds a limitation to the interpretation of the survey result.
It provides numerical proof that the survey was biased.
It restates the survey result without modification.
It changes the topic from public opinion to economics.
questions.explanation: The sentence explains what the first survey could not establish.

questions.text: A passage compares two methods for preserving fruit: drying and freezing. It describes the cost, energy use, and texture effects of each method before concluding that the better method depends on the intended use. Which structure is most accurate?
options: Comparison of alternatives followed by a conditional conclusion.
Chronological sequence followed by a historical claim.
Problem and solution in which only one method is considered.
Definition followed by an unrelated anecdote.
questions.explanation: The passage compares two options across criteria and then gives a nuanced conclusion.

questions.text: A historian notes that early maps of a coastline differ substantially from modern satellite measurements. She then explains that the early maps were often drawn from brief shipboard observations. Finally, she argues that the differences should not automatically be treated as evidence that the coastline itself changed. What is the function of the middle sentence?
options: It offers a possible explanation for the discrepancy introduced in the first sentence.
It proves that the coastline never changed.
It gives an example of a modern satellite measurement.
It introduces a second discrepancy unrelated to mapping.
questions.explanation: The middle sentence explains why early maps may differ, setting up the historian’s caution in the final sentence.

questions.text: A text first describes a puzzling pattern in which some birds arrive earlier each spring. It next considers warmer temperatures as an explanation, then notes that arrival dates also shifted in years when temperatures did not. The text ends by proposing that changes in food availability may also contribute. Which choice best describes the structure?
options: A pattern is introduced, one explanation is tested against conflicting evidence, and an additional explanation is proposed.
A historical timeline is presented and then summarized.
Two bird species are compared without discussing causes.
A conclusion is stated first and all later evidence simply repeats it.
questions.explanation: The passage tests a possible cause, finds it incomplete, and adds another factor.

questions.text: A critic writes that a novel’s narrator frequently claims to be objective. The critic then quotes several moments in which the narrator uses emotionally loaded descriptions. The critic concludes that the narrator’s self-presentation should be treated cautiously. What is the function of the quotations?
options: They provide textual evidence that supports the critic’s conclusion.
They define the meaning of objectivity.
questions.explanation: The quoted language directly supports the critic’s claim that the narrator is not fully objective.

questions.text: A passage explains a conservation policy, describes a short-term rise in the target animal’s population, then notes that the population later declined when habitat quality worsened. The author concludes that population counts alone are insufficient for evaluating the policy. Which structural description is best?
options: A policy is introduced, an apparent success is complicated by later evidence, and a broader evaluation criterion is proposed.
A definition is followed by several unrelated statistics.
A chronological history is presented without interpretation.
Two policies are compared and one is rejected for being too expensive.
questions.explanation: The passage uses later evidence to complicate an initial positive result and revise how success should be judged.

questions.text: A scientist introduces a model predicting that a certain chemical reaction should speed up as pressure increases. She then reports that the prediction holds at low pressures but fails above a threshold. The final paragraph discusses a second mechanism that becomes important at high pressure. What role does the final paragraph play?
options: It offers an explanation for the model’s limited range of success.
It restates the original prediction without change.
It argues that pressure never affects the reaction.
It provides historical background unrelated to the experiment.
questions.explanation: The second mechanism accounts for why the original model stops working at high pressure.

questions.text:
A school compared average quiz scores before and after introducing a daily review routine. Which statement is best supported by the table?
Subject Before After
Math 72 81
Science 75 80
History 78 79
options: All three subjects improved, with Math showing the largest increase.
Science scores decreased after the routine.
Math and Science improved by the same number of points.
questions.explanation: Math rises 9 points, Science 5, History 1; all increase and Math increases most.

questions.text:
The table shows plant height after four weeks under three light conditions. Which claim is supported?
Light condition Mean height (cm)
Low 12
Medium 18
High 17
options: The tallest plants, on average, were grown under medium light.
High light produced plants twice as tall as low light.
Low and high light produced equal heights.
Height increased continuously as light increased.
questions.explanation: Medium light has the highest mean height, 18 cm.

questions.text:
A researcher claims that attendance generally increased from March to May. Which data best support the claim?
Month Attendance
March 210
April 235
May 260
options: Attendance rose each month from 210 to 260.
Attendance fell by 50 from March to May.
questions.explanation: The values increase each month: 210, 235, 260.

questions.text:
Which statement is true according to the table?
Team Wins Losses
A 12 8
B 15 5
C 10 10
options: Team B had the most wins.
Team C had fewer losses than Team B.
Team A and Team C had the same number of wins.
Team A won more games than Team B.
questions.explanation: Team B has 15 wins, more than A or C.

questions.text:
A student says that Group X had a higher mean score than Group Y. Which table entry directly supports that statement?
Group Mean score Sample size
X 84 40
Y 79 60
questions.explanation: The claim compares means, so the relevant values are 84 and 79.

questions.text:
A report claims that the new bus route reduced average travel time more for Route A than for Route B. Which choice best supports the claim?
Route Before (min) After (min)
A 48 35
B 42 36
options: Route A decreased by 13 minutes, while Route B decreased by 6 minutes.
Route B had a shorter trip than Route A before the change.
Both routes had travel times above 30 minutes after the change.
Route A had a longer trip than Route B before the change.
questions.explanation: The size of the reductions directly addresses the claim.

questions.text:
A scientist argues that Treatment P appears most effective at reducing colony size. Which statement best supports the argument?
Treatment Initial colonies Final colonies
P 100 35
Q 100 58
R 100 61
options: P had the lowest final colony count.
R had 61 colonies at the end.
Q and R both reduced colony size.
questions.explanation: Because starting counts are equal, P’s lowest final count indicates the largest reduction.

questions.text:
A passage claims that the relationship between study time and score is positive but not perfectly consistent. Which data pattern best matches the claim?
Hours studied Score
1 62
2 70
3 68
4 79
5 85
options: Scores generally rise as study time increases, though the 3-hour score dips below the 2-hour score.
Scores decrease every time study hours increase.
Every additional hour produces exactly 8 more points.
The highest score occurs at 1 hour.
questions.explanation: The overall direction is upward, but there is a local exception at 3 hours.

questions.text:
A researcher claims that City M had the greatest percentage increase in bike commuting. Which choice is supported?
City 2020 (%) 2025 (%)
M 4 8
N 8 12
P 10 13
options: City M doubled from 4% to 8%, a 100% increase.
City P had the lowest 2025 percentage.
City M had the largest absolute 2025 percentage.
questions.explanation: M increases by 4 on a base of 4, which is 100%; N rises 50%, P 30%.

questions.text:
A claim states that Product A became more expensive while Product B became cheaper. Which row supports the claim?
Product January June
A $20 $24
B $18 $15
C $25 $25
options: A rose by $4 and B fell by $3.
A and B both rose in price.
B was always more expensive than A.
questions.explanation: A increases and B decreases, exactly matching the claim.

questions.text:
A researcher argues that increasing sample size is associated with a smaller margin of error. Which evidence best supports the claim?
Sample size Margin of error
100 ±9%
400 ±4.5%
900 ±3%
options: The margin of error decreases as sample size increases.
The largest sample has the largest margin of error.
The margin of error is identical for all samples.
questions.explanation: The table shows a clear inverse relationship between sample size and margin of error.

questions.text:
A text claims that Species A is more tolerant of high temperatures than Species B because A maintains activity while B’s activity falls sharply. Which choice best supports the claim?
Temperature Species A activity Species B activity
20°C 90 92
30°C 88 75
40°C 82 31
options: At 40°C, A remains at 82 while B falls to 31.
At 20°C, B is slightly more active than A.
A decreases from 90 to 88 between 20°C and 30°C.
questions.explanation: The 40°C comparison most directly shows A maintaining activity while B collapses.

questions.text:
A writer argues that the new policy narrowed, but did not eliminate, the performance gap between two groups. Which evidence best supports the statement?
Group Before policy After policy
X 88 90
Y 72 82
options: The gap decreased from 16 points to 8 points.
Both groups had identical scores after the policy.
Group X decreased after the policy.
The gap increased from 8 points to 16 points.
questions.explanation: Before: 88-72=16; after: 90-82=8. The gap is smaller but still present.

questions.text:
A researcher claims that a treatment’s effect may level off at higher doses. Which pattern best supports the claim?
Dose (mg) Response
0 10
5 24
10 35
15 39
20 40
options: The response gains become progressively smaller at the highest doses.
The response decreases at every dose.
The response is unchanged from 0 to 20 mg.
The largest increase occurs from 15 to 20 mg.
questions.explanation: Increases shrink from +14, +11, +4, to +1, showing leveling off.

questions.text:
A claim says that Region C had the highest total output across two years even though it did not lead in either single year. Which choice is supported?
Region Year 1 Year 2
A 60 30
B 35 62
C 50 50
options: C totals 100, higher than A’s 90 and B’s 97.
C has the highest value in Year 1.
C has the highest value in Year 2.
A and B have identical two-year totals.
questions.explanation: C’s combined total is 100, even though A leads Year 1 and B leads Year 2.

questions.text: If f(x)=3x+5, what is f(4)?
Which of the following is a factor of x^2-9?
If x=2 is a zero of polynomial p(x), which expression must be a factor of p(x)?
questions.explanation: A zero at x=2 corresponds to factor x-2.

questions.text: A polynomial has degree 4. What is the greatest possible number of real zeros it can have?
questions.explanation: A degree-4 polynomial can have at most 4 real zeros.

questions.text: The graph of g(x)=f(x)+6 is obtained from the graph of f(x) by shifting it
questions.explanation: Adding 6 outside the function shifts the graph vertically upward by 6.

questions.text: If p(x)=x^2-5x+6, what is p(3)?
questions.explanation: p(3)=9-15+6=0, so x-3 is a factor.

questions.text: Which factored form has zeros at -4 and 7?
questions.explanation: Zero -4 gives x+4; zero 7 gives x-7.

questions.text: For f(x)=2(x-1)(x+5), what is the y-intercept?
If f(x)=x^3-2x^2-5x+6 and f(1)=0, what does this show?
options: The polynomial has no real roots
questions.explanation: f(1)=0 means x=1 is a zero, so x-1 is a factor.

questions.text: The graph of h(x)=f(x-5) is the graph of f shifted
questions.explanation: Replacing x with x-5 shifts the graph right 5.

questions.text: A cubic polynomial has zeros at -2, 1, and 5 and leading coefficient 2. Which equation could define it?
questions.explanation: Each zero gives its corresponding factor; leading coefficient 2 multiplies the product.

questions.text: When p(x)=2x^3+3x^2-kx+5 is divided by x-2, the remainder is 7. What is k?
A polynomial q(x) has q(4)=0 and q(-1)=0. Which expression must divide q(x)?
questions.explanation: Zeros 4 and -1 imply factors x-4 and x+1.

questions.text: The function f(x)=a(x-3)(x+2) passes through (0,-12). What is a?
For p(x)=x^4-5x^2+4, which set lists all real zeros?
Claim: Regular exposure to natural environments can reduce reported stress. Which finding would most directly support the claim?
options: Participants who walked in a park reported lower stress afterward than participants who walked beside heavy traffic.
Some participants preferred walking in the morning.
The park contained more trees than the city street.
Participants in both groups walked for the same amount of time.
questions.explanation: The finding directly compares stress outcomes after natural versus urban exposure.

questions.text: Claim: A new coating helps metal resist corrosion. Which evidence best supports the claim?
options: Coated samples showed less rust after saltwater exposure than uncoated samples.
The samples were stored in the same room before testing.
Researchers used metal from two suppliers.
questions.explanation: Less rust in coated samples directly demonstrates corrosion resistance.

questions.text: Claim: The narrator is uncertain about the decision. Which quotation best supports the claim?
options: “I reached for the handle, then stopped, wondering whether I should open the door at all.”
“The door was painted a deep green.”
questions.explanation: The hesitation and wondering directly reveal uncertainty.

questions.text: Claim: The author views the discovery as unexpected. Which quotation best supports the claim?
options: “To the researchers’ surprise, the smallest sample produced the strongest signal.”
questions.explanation: “To the researchers’ surprise” directly indicates unexpectedness.

questions.text: Claim: The policy increased participation. Which evidence is most relevant?
options: Attendance rose from 420 to 610 after the policy began.
The policy was announced on a Tuesday.
The program was held in the same building.
questions.explanation: The attendance increase directly measures participation.

questions.text: Researchers hypothesize that reflective markings make insects harder for predators to detect because reflections break up the insects’ outlines. Which finding would most strongly support the hypothesis?
options: Predators took longer to locate reflective models than otherwise identical nonreflective models.
Reflective models were heavier than nonreflective models.
Predators preferred larger prey in a separate experiment.
Some reflective models were damaged during transport.
questions.explanation: The detection-time difference directly tests the proposed camouflage mechanism.

questions.text: A historian argues that a reform was driven partly by public pressure rather than solely by economic concerns. Which evidence best supports the argument?
options: Letters to lawmakers sharply increased before the reform, and many explicitly demanded the change.
Tax revenue rose in the decade after the reform.
The reform was passed by a narrow margin.
Several lawmakers had backgrounds in business.
questions.explanation: The letters provide direct evidence of organized public pressure before the reform.

questions.text: A critic claims that the poem shifts from confidence to doubt. Which quotation pair best supports the claim?
options: “I know the road before me” followed later by “Yet now each sign seems strange.”
“Morning light filled the room” followed by “Birds crossed the sky.”
“I carried a map” followed by “The map was folded.”
“The road was narrow” followed by “The hill was steep.”
questions.explanation: The first line expresses certainty; the later line signals doubt.

questions.text: Scientists claim that a species can adjust feeding behavior when its preferred food becomes scarce. Which result best supports the claim?
options: When preferred seeds were reduced, the animals increased consumption of an alternative seed type.
The animals ate the preferred seeds fastest when those seeds were abundant.
The alternative seeds contained less protein.
questions.explanation: The shift to alternative food under scarcity directly shows behavioral adjustment.

questions.text: An author argues that a city’s growth was uneven across neighborhoods. Which evidence best supports the argument?
options: Some neighborhoods gained more than 20% in population while others lost population.
The city’s total population increased by 8%.
The city opened three new schools.
The average household size remained stable.
questions.explanation: Contrasting neighborhood-level changes directly demonstrate uneven growth.

questions.text: A researcher claims that the benefit of a tutoring program is unlikely to be explained only by extra study time. Which evidence would most strongly support the claim?
options: Tutored students outperformed a comparison group that spent the same additional amount of time studying independently.
Tutored students reported liking their tutors.
Tutored students studied more than they had the previous semester.
The tutoring sessions took place after school.
questions.skill: Textual evidence - rule out alternative explanation
questions.explanation: Equal extra study time controls for time, so the performance difference points to something about tutoring itself.

questions.text: A literary scholar argues that a character’s apparent generosity is partly strategic. Which quotation best supports the argument?
options: “He offered the gift only after glancing toward the reporters gathered at the doorway.”
“He wrapped the gift in plain paper.”
“He had purchased the gift the previous week.”
questions.explanation: Looking toward reporters before giving the gift suggests concern with public appearance.

questions.text: A study claims that sleep improves memory consolidation rather than merely reducing fatigue during testing. Which finding best supports the claim?
options: Participants who slept after learning remembered more a day later than participants who stayed awake, even though both groups were equally rested at the final test.
Participants who slept reported feeling less tired immediately after waking.
Participants learned the material in the same room.
questions.explanation: Equal rest at testing weakens the fatigue explanation while preserving a memory advantage from sleep.

questions.text: A researcher argues that a rise in average temperature did not affect all regions equally. Which evidence best supports the argument?
options: Northern sites warmed by 2.4°C on average, while coastal sites warmed by only 0.6°C.
The national average temperature rose by 1.3°C.
All sites were measured with the same instruments.
questions.explanation: Different regional changes directly show unequal effects.

questions.text: An economist claims that the decline in sales was more closely associated with reduced consumer demand than with production shortages. Which evidence most strongly supports the claim?
options: Inventories remained high while customer orders fell sharply during the same period.
Several stores changed their opening hours.
questions.explanation: High inventories argue against shortage, while falling orders directly indicate weak demand.

questions.text: A library extended its weekend hours. During the next month, weekend visits increased while weekday visits remained about the same. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The longer weekend hours may have contributed to increased weekend use.
The library became less popular on weekdays.
The library should close on weekdays.
questions.explanation: The timing supports a cautious connection, but not a universal or certain causal claim.

questions.text: A plant species grows naturally only in shaded, moist areas. A newly discovered population is found in a valley with dense tree cover and frequent fog. What can most reasonably be inferred?
options: The valley likely provides conditions suitable for the species.
The species can survive only in fog.
The valley receives no direct sunlight at any time.
The population was planted by humans.
questions.explanation: The known habitat preferences align with the valley’s shaded, moist conditions.

questions.text: A museum reports that a new exhibit sold out every timed-entry slot during its first week. What is the most reasonable inference?
options: Demand for the exhibit was high during its first week.
Every museum visitor preferred the new exhibit to all others.
The museum earned a profit that week.
The exhibit will remain sold out for a year.
questions.explanation: Selling out slots supports high initial demand, not broader claims about preference, profit, or future demand.

questions.text: A study finds that birds on noisier streets begin singing earlier in the morning than birds in quieter areas. Which inference is most supported?
options: Street noise may be associated with changes in singing time.
Noise always causes birds to sing louder.
Birds on quiet streets cannot hear one another.
All bird species respond to noise in the same way.
questions.explanation: The study supports an association with timing, not universal causation or other behaviors.

questions.text: An author notes that a manuscript contains corrections in two different inks and handwriting styles. What is a reasonable inference?
options: More than one person may have revised the manuscript.
The manuscript was written in two different centuries.
questions.explanation: Different inks and handwriting reasonably suggest multiple revisers, while stronger claims are unsupported.

questions.text: A company’s remote employees completed slightly more projects on average, but they also had more years of experience than office employees. Which inference is most justified?
options: The productivity difference cannot confidently be attributed to remote work alone.
Remote work definitely causes higher productivity.
Experience has no relationship to productivity.
questions.explanation: Experience differs between groups, so it could partly explain the observed productivity difference.

questions.text: After a wet spring, a lake’s algae population increased sharply. Nutrient runoff from nearby farms also increased that spring. Which inference is most reasonable?
options: Increased runoff may have contributed to the algae increase, but the evidence does not prove it was the only cause.
Runoff was certainly the sole cause of the algae increase.
questions.explanation: The correlation and plausible mechanism support a possible contribution, not sole causation.

questions.text: A novelist repeatedly describes a character checking the clock during a conversation and giving increasingly brief answers. What can reasonably be inferred?
options: The character is becoming impatient or eager to leave.
The character has forgotten the time.
The conversation is taking place at midnight.
questions.explanation: Repeated time-checking and shorter answers support impatience/eagerness to leave.

questions.text: Researchers find that two populations of the same fish species have different average body sizes. The populations also live in waters with different temperatures and food supplies. What is the best inference?
options: Environmental differences could be related to the size difference, but the data alone do not identify which factor matters.
Temperature is definitely the only cause.
Food supply cannot affect body size.
questions.explanation: Several environmental variables differ, so the evidence does not isolate one cause.

questions.text: A city installed protected bike lanes on three streets. Bicycle counts increased on those streets but not on nearby streets without new lanes. Which inference is most supported?
options: The protected lanes may have encouraged more cycling on the treated streets.
The lanes caused every resident to begin cycling.
Cycling decreased everywhere else in the city.
The nearby streets were unsafe before the change.
questions.explanation: The contrasting pattern supports a cautious inference that the lanes contributed to increased cycling.

questions.text: A study reports that students who voluntarily attended review sessions scored higher than those who did not. No students were randomly assigned to attend. Which inference is most justified?
options: The results show an association, but motivated students may have been more likely to attend, so causation is uncertain.
The sessions definitely caused the score increase.
Review sessions have no academic benefit.
Random assignment would guarantee identical scores.
questions.explanation: Self-selection can confound the association, preventing a strong causal conclusion.

questions.text: Archaeologists find imported pottery at a coastal settlement but no written trade records. Similar pottery is common at a distant port. Which inference is reasonable?
options: The settlement likely had some direct or indirect exchange connection with regions where the pottery circulated.
The settlement definitely traded directly with that exact port.
The pottery was manufactured at the settlement.
questions.explanation: Imported pottery supports exchange, but not the exact route or direct trading partner.

questions.text: A medicine reduces symptoms in a trial, but the treatment group also received more frequent check-ins from clinicians than the control group. Which inference is best?
options: The symptom difference may reflect the medicine, the extra attention, or both.
The control group must have received a placebo with active ingredients.
questions.explanation: Because two factors differ, the observed outcome cannot be attributed uniquely to the medicine.

questions.text: A historian finds that newspaper editorials became more supportive of a policy shortly after a major public event. Private letters from editors are unavailable. What can reasonably be inferred?
options: The event may have influenced public editorial positions, but the editors’ private motives cannot be established from the evidence.
The event definitely changed every editor’s personal beliefs.
The editors were ordered by the government to support the policy.
The editorials were not read by the public.
questions.skill: Inference - public evidence vs private motive
questions.explanation: The timing supports possible influence on published positions, but motives remain unknown.

questions.text: A species appears in the fossil record immediately after a major environmental change, but the fossil record from the preceding period is sparse. Which inference is best supported?
options: The species may have emerged or expanded then, but the sparse earlier record makes the exact timing uncertain.
The species certainly evolved on the exact date of the environmental change.
The environmental change had no effect on the species.
The species did not exist anywhere before the change.
questions.explanation: Sparse earlier evidence limits certainty about first appearance and causation.

questions.text: What is the mean of 6, 8, 10, and 12?
What is the median of 3, 5, 8, 11, 14?
questions.explanation: The middle of five ordered values is 8.

questions.text: What is the range of 4, 9, 12, 15?
Which data set has the smaller standard deviation?
questions.explanation: All values are identical in A, so its spread and standard deviation are 0.

questions.text: If a survey’s sample size increases substantially while the sampling method stays similar, what generally happens to the margin of error?
options: It is unaffected by sample size.
questions.explanation: Larger samples generally reduce sampling uncertainty and margin of error.

questions.text: The data set is 4, 7, 7, 9, 13. If 13 is replaced by 18, which statistic definitely increases?
questions.skill: Effect of changing an extreme value
questions.explanation: Median stays 7; range rises from 9 to 14.

questions.text: Two data sets have the same mean. Set A is tightly clustered around the mean, while Set B contains values much farther from the mean. Which statement is true?
options: Set A has the larger standard deviation.
Set B has the larger standard deviation.
The standard deviations must be equal.
questions.explanation: Greater spread from the mean means greater standard deviation.

questions.text: A box plot has minimum 12, Q1=18, median=25, Q3=31, maximum=44. What is the interquartile range?
A data set of 5 numbers has mean 20. Four of the numbers are 12, 18, 21, and 24. What is the fifth number?
questions.explanation: Total must be 100. Known sum is 75, so missing value is 25.

questions.text: A poll of 100 voters has a margin of error of ±10 percentage points. A similar poll uses 400 voters. Which margin of error is most plausible?
questions.explanation: Quadrupling sample size roughly halves margin of error because MOE scales with 1/sqrt(n).

questions.text: Set A: 20,20,20,40,40. Set B: 10,20,30,40,40. Which statement is true?
options: Both sets have the same mean, and Set B has a larger range.
Both sets have the same mean, and Set A has a larger range.
Set A has a larger mean and a larger range.
Set B has a larger mean and a smaller range.
questions.explanation: Both sums are 140, so both means are 28. A range=20; B range=30.

questions.text: A class has 20 students with mean score 75. A second class has 30 students with mean score 85. What is the combined mean?
questions.explanation: Combined total=20(75)+30(85)=4050; divide by 50 gives 81.

questions.text: A box plot for Group A has Q1=40 and Q3=60. Group B has Q1=45 and Q3=55. Which statement is best supported?
options: The middle 50% of Group A is more spread out than the middle 50% of Group B.
Group B must have a larger overall range.
Group A must have a larger mean.
questions.explanation: A’s IQR is 20; B’s is 10, so A’s middle half is more dispersed.

questions.text: A survey estimate is 52% with a margin of error of ±4 percentage points. Which value is outside the reported interval?
questions.explanation: The interval is 48% to 56%; 58% is outside.

questions.text: Data set A has mean 50 and standard deviation 2. Data set B has mean 50 and standard deviation 12. Which claim is best supported?
options: B’s values are generally more dispersed around 50 than A’s.
B must contain a larger number of data points.
A must have a larger range than B.
The medians of both sets must be 50.
questions.explanation: With equal means, the larger SD indicates greater typical spread around 50.

questions.text: A research team tracked monarch butterflies during migration. The researchers found that butterflies released on clear days generally flew southwest, while butterflies released under heavy cloud cover showed less consistent direction. According to the text, what happened when butterflies were released under heavy cloud cover?
questions.explanation: The text directly states that butterflies released under heavy cloud cover showed less consistent direction.

questions.text: A museum replaced several incandescent display bulbs with LED bulbs. After the change, electricity use in the gallery decreased by 28 percent, while visitor attendance remained about the same. According to the text, what changed after the museum installed LED bulbs?
questions.explanation: The only reported change is a 28 percent decrease in electricity use.

questions.text: Astronomers observing a distant star recorded small, regular drops in the star's brightness every 4.2 days. They concluded that an orbiting planet was likely passing in front of the star. According to the text, how often did the recorded drops occur?
questions.explanation: The passage gives a specific interval of 4.2 days.

questions.text: In a field study, ecologists placed identical trays of seeds in open grassland and beneath dense shrubs. Birds removed more seeds from the open trays than from the trays under shrubs. According to the text, from which trays did birds remove more seeds?
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says birds removed more seeds from the open trays.

questions.text: A city library extended its weekend hours from four hours to seven hours per day. During the following month, weekend visits increased, but weekday visits stayed nearly unchanged. According to the text, which visits stayed nearly unchanged?
questions.explanation: The passage states that weekday visits stayed nearly unchanged.

questions.text: Biologists studying a coastal marsh compared two restoration sites. Site A was planted with native grasses and received regular tidal flow. Site B was planted with the same grasses but was separated from tidal flow by a berm. After two years, plant survival was substantially higher at Site A. Which detail from the text is most relevant to explaining the difference in plant survival?
options: Both sites were located in a coastal marsh.
Both sites were planted with native grasses.
Only Site A received regular tidal flow.
questions.explanation: The key difference between the sites is tidal flow; the other listed details are shared or merely contextual.

questions.text: A study compared students who reviewed vocabulary for ten minutes each day with students who reviewed the same total amount of time in one weekly session. After six weeks, the daily-review group remembered more words on a delayed test. According to the text, what was the same for both groups?
options: The number of weeks they studied each day
questions.explanation: The text says both groups spent the same total amount of review time, but distributed it differently.

questions.text: A historian notes that a 1910 newspaper praised a new railway for reducing travel time between two cities. The historian also points out that ticket prices remained too high for many working-class families. Which statement is directly supported by the text?
options: The railway reduced travel time but was not affordable for everyone.
The railway was slower than earlier transportation.
Working-class families opposed all railway construction.
questions.explanation: Both parts of A are directly stated: shorter travel time and limited affordability.

questions.text: Researchers tested two types of insulation in identical model houses. House X lost 12 percent of its heat over one hour, whereas House Y lost 19 percent. Both houses began at the same indoor temperature. Which detail is necessary for a fair comparison of heat loss?
options: The houses began at the same indoor temperature.
House Y lost 19 percent of its heat.
The insulation types had different names.
questions.explanation: Starting at the same indoor temperature is a control that makes the comparison meaningful.

questions.text: A passage explains that a composer wrote an early version of a symphony in 1898, revised the orchestration in 1905, and approved a shortened performance edition in 1912. According to the text, what happened second?
questions.explanation: The sequence given is 1898 writing, 1905 revision, 1912 approval.

questions.text: A linguist examined recordings from three communities where the same language is spoken. Younger speakers in Community A increasingly used a new vowel pronunciation; younger speakers in Community B used it only occasionally; speakers of all ages in Community C rarely used it. Which statement is directly supported by the text?
options: The new pronunciation is equally common in all three communities.
In Community A, the new pronunciation is more associated with younger speakers.
Older speakers in Community B use the pronunciation more often than younger speakers do.
Community C created the new pronunciation.
questions.explanation: The text specifically associates increasing use in Community A with younger speakers. The other claims add unsupported information.

questions.text: A study of urban trees reported that trees along streets with wider planting strips had larger average trunk diameters than trees in narrow strips. The researchers cautioned, however, that the wider strips were also more common on streets with less vehicle traffic. Which detail most directly limits the conclusion that strip width alone caused the difference in trunk diameter?
options: The study focused on urban trees.
Trunk diameter was measured as an average.
Wider strips were more common where vehicle traffic was lower.
Some streets had narrow planting strips.
questions.explanation: Traffic level differs along with strip width, so it could also contribute to the observed tree-size difference.

questions.text: An archaeologist compares two settlements. Settlement P contains imported pottery dated to 400-450 CE and local pottery from a much wider period. Settlement Q contains no imported pottery but has local pottery dated to 430-470 CE. Which statement is supported by the evidence given?
options: Settlement P was occupied only from 400 to 450 CE.
Settlement Q definitely had no contact with other regions.
Some activity at the two settlements may have overlapped in time.
Settlement P is older than every artifact at Settlement Q.
questions.explanation: The date ranges overlap from about 430 to 450 CE. The other choices overstate what the pottery can prove.

questions.text: A passage reports that a medication reduced average symptom scores more than a placebo did. It also notes that participants taking the medication reported side effects more frequently. Which detail is most important when evaluating whether the medication offers an overall advantage?
options: The balance between symptom improvement and side effects
The color of the placebo tablets
The number of letters in the symptom scale
questions.explanation: Both the benefit and the increased side effects are directly relevant to evaluating the treatment overall.

questions.text: A climate study found that Mountain Station R had lower average temperatures than Valley Station S in every month measured. Station R, however, was also located 1,400 meters higher in elevation. Which statement is directly supported by the text without making a causal claim?
options: Higher elevation always causes lower temperatures.
Station R was cooler than Station S during every measured month.
Station S would become cooler if moved uphill.
Elevation was the only difference between the stations.
questions.explanation: B simply restates the observed pattern. The other options claim causation or exclusivity not established by the text.

questions.text: Community gardens are often valued for providing fresh produce. They can also create shaded areas, absorb rainwater, and give neighbors a place to meet. For these reasons, some city planners now view community gardens as useful infrastructure rather than simply recreational spaces. Which choice best states the central idea of the text?
options: Community gardens can serve several practical and social functions in cities.
Fresh produce is the only important benefit of community gardens.
City planners generally oppose community gardens.
Rainwater is the main problem facing all cities.
questions.explanation: A captures the full passage: gardens provide food, environmental benefits, and social value.

questions.text: For many years, scientists assumed that octopuses changed color mainly to hide from predators. More recent observations show that some color changes occur during interactions with other octopuses, suggesting that color may also play a role in communication. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Octopuses never use color for camouflage.
Octopus color change may serve communication as well as camouflage.
All octopus communication depends on color.
questions.explanation: The passage broadens the function of color change from camouflage alone to possible communication as well.

questions.text: A small town converted an abandoned rail corridor into a walking and cycling path. Local businesses near the path later reported more visitors, and residents gained a safer route between neighborhoods. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: The rail corridor should have remained unused.
The new path provided transportation and economic benefits.
Local businesses caused the rail line to close.
Cycling is always safer than driving.
questions.explanation: B summarizes both the safer route and increased business visits.

questions.text: Researchers have found that sleep supports memory consolidation, a process by which newly learned information becomes more stable. Students who sleep after studying often remember more the next day than students kept awake for the same period. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Sleep can help stabilize newly learned information.
Studying is unnecessary if a student sleeps enough.
Students should always study at night.
Memory disappears when people stay awake.
questions.explanation: The text explains that sleep contributes to memory consolidation and better retention.

questions.text: Some desert plants produce seeds that can remain dormant for years. When unusually heavy rain arrives, many of these seeds germinate quickly, allowing the plants to reproduce during brief favorable conditions. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Desert plants cannot reproduce during dry periods.
Dormant seeds help some desert plants take advantage of rare rainfall.
Heavy rain permanently changes desert climates.
All seeds germinate immediately after they form.
questions.explanation: B captures the adaptation and why it is useful.

questions.text: Early maps of ocean currents were based largely on sailors' observations of ship drift. Today, satellites measure sea-surface height and temperature across vast regions, allowing scientists to track currents much more systematically. Although the tools have changed, both approaches use patterns in movement to understand the ocean. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Modern satellite methods have made all historical observations useless.
Scientists have used different kinds of observations over time to study ocean currents.
Sailors understood ocean currents better than modern scientists do.
Sea-surface temperature is the only useful measure of ocean currents.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts old and new methods while emphasizing their shared goal of understanding currents through observed patterns.

questions.text: A species of frog was once thought to live only in lowland forest. Surveys conducted at higher elevations have now identified several small populations there as well. The discoveries do not show that the species is common at high elevations, but they do suggest that its habitat range is broader than researchers previously believed. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: The frog is equally common at all elevations.
New surveys have expanded scientists' understanding of the frog's habitat range.
Lowland forests are unsuitable for the frog.
Researchers have proved that the frog prefers high elevations.
questions.explanation: B reflects the new evidence and the passage's caution about abundance.

questions.text: In many orchestras, musicians tune to a reference pitch before performing. This practice does not guarantee that every note in the concert will be perfectly in tune; temperature, instrument design, and playing technique can all affect pitch. Still, using a shared reference gives the ensemble a common starting point. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: A reference pitch helps coordinate tuning even though other factors can still affect pitch.
Temperature has no effect on musical instruments.
Orchestras should tune repeatedly during every song.
Reference pitches make tuning errors impossible.
questions.explanation: The passage describes a useful but limited role for a shared reference pitch.

questions.text: Economists sometimes use average income to describe a region's prosperity. However, two regions with the same average income can have very different distributions of wealth. For that reason, researchers often examine median income and inequality measures alongside the average. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Average income should never be calculated.
A single average may not fully describe how income is distributed.
Median income is always higher than average income.
All regions with the same average income are equally prosperous.
questions.skill: Central idea - limitation of a measure
questions.explanation: The passage argues that average income alone can conceal distributional differences.

questions.text: For decades, engineers designed flood barriers primarily to block water from entering cities. Some newer projects instead create parks and wetlands that temporarily store floodwater while also providing habitat and public space. These projects reflect a shift from resisting water entirely to managing where it can safely go. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Modern flood management can combine water storage with ecological and public benefits.
Wetlands should replace every form of urban infrastructure.
Public parks are the main cause of flooding.
questions.explanation: A captures the shift toward multifunctional flood management.

questions.text: A historian studying early photography notes that long exposure times made candid street scenes difficult to capture. As cameras became more sensitive, photographers could record movement more easily, and urban photographs increasingly included workers, traffic, and spontaneous public activity. The historian argues that this technical change affected not only how photographs were made but also what kinds of city life entered the historical record. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Improved camera technology expanded the kinds of urban activity that photography could document.
Early photographers were uninterested in city life.
Workers appeared in photographs only after traffic increased.
Long exposure times made all nineteenth-century photographs inaccurate.
questions.explanation: The passage connects technical improvements with a broader change in what urban life could be recorded.

questions.text: Some ecologists once treated small forest patches as having little conservation value because they support fewer species than large forests. More recent work, however, shows that networks of small patches can function as stepping-stones between larger habitats, helping some animals move across fragmented landscapes. The findings do not make small patches equivalent to large forests, but they complicate the idea that small patches are unimportant. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Small forest patches can contribute to connectivity even though they do not replace large forests.
Small forest patches always contain more species than large forests.
Large forests are unnecessary if small patches are protected.
Animals avoid fragmented landscapes under all conditions.
questions.explanation: A preserves both points: small patches matter for connectivity, but they are not equivalent to large forests.

questions.text: A literary scholar argues that a novelist's frequent shifts between first-person diary entries and third-person narration are not merely stylistic decoration. The diary entries restrict readers to one character's immediate knowledge, whereas the third-person sections reveal events that character cannot see. By alternating the two modes, the novel repeatedly changes how much information the reader has. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: The novel's changes in narrative perspective control the reader's access to information.
The diary entries are more accurate than the third-person sections.
The novelist uses first person because third person is difficult to write.
The novel contains no events outside the diarist's experience.
questions.explanation: The main point is that alternating perspectives changes how much the reader knows.

questions.text: Researchers studying a fish population found that individuals in warmer water grew faster during their first year but reached smaller adult sizes. The result illustrates a broader biological trade-off: conditions that accelerate early growth do not necessarily maximize size later in life. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Faster early growth can be associated with a later cost in adult size.
Warm water always harms fish at every life stage.
Adult fish size is determined only by first-year growth.
questions.explanation: A states the general trade-off illustrated by the specific fish result.

questions.text: A political scientist compares two measures of voter participation. Turnout as a percentage of registered voters is easy to calculate but excludes eligible citizens who never registered. Turnout as a percentage of the voting-age population includes many noncitizens who cannot vote. The researcher concludes that each measure answers a slightly different question and must be interpreted with its denominator in mind. Which choice best states the central idea?
options: Different turnout measures have different limitations because they use different comparison groups.
Registered-voter turnout is always the most accurate measure.
Voting-age population figures include only citizens.
All turnout measures produce identical results.
questions.explanation: The passage compares denominator choices and explains why each measure must be interpreted accordingly.

questions.text: A jar contains 7 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. If one marble is selected at random, what is the probability that it is blue?
questions.explanation: There are 3 favorable outcomes out of 10 total marbles.

questions.text: A class has 12 students who play a sport and 8 students who do not. One student is selected at random. What is the probability the student plays a sport?
questions.explanation: 12 of 20 students play a sport, so the probability is 12/20=3/5.

questions.text: A scatterplot shows points clustered around an upward-sloping line. Which relationship is most likely?
questions.explanation: An upward trend indicates that larger x-values tend to be associated with larger y-values.

questions.text: A line of best fit for a scatterplot is y=2x+5. What value of y does the model predict when x=4?
questions.explanation: Substitute x=4: y=2(4)+5=13.

questions.text: A researcher wants to estimate the average commute time of all adults in a city. Which sample is most likely to be representative?
options: Adults leaving one downtown office building
Adults randomly selected from neighborhoods throughout the city
Only adults who commute by bicycle
questions.explanation: A random citywide sample is less likely to be biased toward one location or commuting type.

questions.text: At a school, 30 students are in the robotics club. Of those 30, 18 are juniors. If one robotics-club member is selected at random, what is the probability that the student is a junior?
questions.explanation: The condition "robotics-club member" makes 30 the denominator; 18/30=3/5.

questions.text: A survey of 500 randomly selected city residents finds that 62% support a proposed park. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
options: Exactly 62% of every neighborhood supports the park.
About 62% of city residents may support the park, subject to sampling uncertainty.
The survey proves that 62% of all people in the country support the park.
Every respondent who supports the park lives near it.
questions.explanation: A random city sample may support a citywide estimate, but not exact subgroup or national claims.

questions.text: The line of best fit for a data set is y=0.8x+12. What does the slope 0.8 represent?
options: The model predicts y will decrease by 0.8 for each 1-unit increase in x.
The model predicts y will increase by 0.8 for each 1-unit increase in x.
The model predicts y=0.8 when x=0.
The model predicts x will always equal 12.
questions.explanation: The slope is the predicted change in y per 1-unit increase in x.

questions.text: A scatterplot has a strong negative association. Which description best matches the pattern?
options: As x increases, y tends to decrease.
As x increases, y tends to increase.
y stays exactly constant for all x.
The points form a perfect circle.
questions.explanation: A negative association means higher x-values tend to be paired with lower y-values.

questions.text: A data set has one point far above the rest of the scatterplot. After that point is removed, the line of best fit becomes much less steep. What does this indicate?
options: The removed point had little influence on the model.
The removed point was influential and affected the fitted slope.
All remaining points must be identical.
The original scatterplot had no association.
questions.explanation: A large change in slope after removing one point shows that the point strongly influenced the regression.

questions.text: In a survey, 80 students take Math, 50 take Physics, and 30 take both. If a student is chosen at random from the 80 Math students, what is the probability that the student also takes Physics?
questions.explanation: Given that the student takes Math, the denominator is 80; 30/80=3/8.

questions.text: A scatterplot models the relationship between hours of weekly practice x and a performance score y. The line of best fit is y=4.5x+62. A student practices 6 hours and scores 84. Which statement is correct?
options: The model predicts 89, so the student scored 5 points below the prediction.
The model predicts 89, so the student scored 5 points above the prediction.
The model predicts 66.5, so the student scored 17.5 points above the prediction.
questions.explanation: Predicted y=4.5(6)+62=89. The actual score 84 is 5 below prediction.

questions.text: A researcher surveys 2,000 customers who voluntarily responded to a link printed on receipts and finds that 91% are satisfied. Which limitation most directly affects generalizing the result to all customers?
options: Voluntary responders may differ systematically from customers who did not respond.
Percentages cannot be used in surveys.
questions.explanation: Voluntary response can create selection bias even with a large sample.

questions.text: A scatterplot contains points that generally follow an upward trend. One extreme point lies far to the right and far below that trend. Which effect is most plausible if the extreme point is included in a linear regression?
options: It may reduce the estimated positive slope.
It must make the slope exactly zero.
It cannot affect the fitted line.
questions.explanation: A high-x, low-y point pulls the right side of the regression line downward, often reducing a positive slope.

questions.text: A study finds a positive association between neighborhood tree cover and average household income. Which conclusion is best supported by the scatterplot alone?
options: Increasing tree cover will necessarily cause household income to rise.
Higher-income neighborhoods in the data tend to have more tree cover, but the graph alone does not establish causation.
Tree cover has no relationship with income.
Income causes trees to grow faster.
questions.explanation: A scatterplot can show association but does not by itself prove the direction or existence of causation.

questions.text:
Text 1: A city planner argues that adding protected bike lanes can make cycling safer and encourage more residents to ride.
Text 2: A public-health researcher notes that cities with connected bike networks often see more people choosing bicycles for short trips.
Which statement would both authors most likely agree with?
options: Cycling infrastructure can influence whether people choose to bicycle.
Protected bike lanes eliminate all traffic injuries.
Cars should be prohibited from city centers.
Only experienced cyclists use bike lanes.
questions.explanation: Both texts connect cycling infrastructure with increased cycling use.

questions.text:
Text 1: A botanist argues that urban rooftop gardens can provide habitat for insects.
Text 2: An architect emphasizes that rooftop gardens can also reduce heat absorbed by buildings.
Which choice best describes a difference between the texts?
options: Text 1 focuses on habitat benefits, while Text 2 focuses on building-temperature benefits.
Text 1 opposes rooftop gardens, while Text 2 supports them.
Text 1 discusses rural farms, while Text 2 discusses forests.
Both texts make exactly the same claim.
questions.explanation: The authors emphasize different benefits of the same intervention.

questions.text:
Text 1: A historian claims that letters written by soldiers are valuable because they reveal individual experiences of war.
Text 2: Another historian warns that personal letters may not represent the experiences of all soldiers.
How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1?
options: By agreeing that letters are useful but cautioning against treating them as fully representative.
By arguing that letters contain no historical information.
By claiming that all soldiers had identical experiences.
By saying that personal documents should never be studied.
questions.explanation: Text 2 qualifies, rather than rejects, the value described in Text 1.

questions.text:
Text 1: Solar panels generate electricity without burning fuel during operation.
Text 2: Wind turbines also generate electricity without burning fuel during operation.
Which statement would both authors agree with?
options: Some renewable technologies can generate electricity without fuel combustion during operation.
Solar power is always cheaper than wind power.
Wind turbines require no materials to build.
Renewable energy works only in cities.
questions.explanation: The shared point is electricity generation without burning fuel during operation.

questions.text:
Text 1: A critic praises a novel for its detailed descriptions of city life.
Text 2: Another critic praises the same novel for its fast-moving plot.
Which choice best describes the relationship between the texts?
options: They value different features of the same novel.
They disagree about whether the novel exists.
Text 1 discusses a film and Text 2 a novel.
Both criticize the novel for being too long.
questions.explanation: The texts are both positive but focus on different qualities.

questions.text:
Text 1: Ecologist Mira Chen argues that reintroducing beavers can restore wetlands because beaver dams slow water and create ponds.
Text 2: Ecologist Jonah Reed agrees that beavers can create wetlands but warns that dams may flood roads or farmland in some locations.
Which statement would both authors most likely agree with?
options: Beaver dams can substantially alter local water conditions.
Flooding from beaver dams is never a concern.
Wetlands can form only when beavers are present.
questions.skill: Paired passages - both agree with qualification
questions.explanation: Both accept that beaver dams modify hydrology; they differ on how desirable that is in all locations.

questions.text:
Text 1: A linguist argues that texting has encouraged creative abbreviation and new written conventions.
Text 2: Another linguist notes that informal digital writing changes rapidly but says this does not imply that formal writing skills are disappearing.
How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
options: By accepting that digital writing develops new conventions while resisting broader claims about language decline.
By denying that texting involves written language.
By claiming that formal writing has already disappeared.
By arguing that abbreviations existed only before digital communication.
questions.explanation: Text 2 can accept innovation in texting but explicitly resists a decline narrative.

questions.text:
Text 1: A study concludes that planting street trees reduced summer surface temperatures on the blocks examined.
Text 2: A researcher notes that tree-planting studies often differ in climate, species, and street design, so results from one city should not automatically be generalized to all cities.
Which choice best describes the difference between the texts?
options: Text 1 reports a specific result; Text 2 emphasizes limits on generalizing such results.
Text 1 rejects tree planting; Text 2 promotes it.
Text 1 studies winter temperatures; Text 2 studies rainfall.
Both texts claim that one city represents every city.
questions.explanation: Text 1 gives a local finding, while Text 2 focuses on external validity and generalization.

questions.text:
Text 1: An economist argues that remote work can reduce commuting time for employees.
Text 2: A management researcher argues that remote work can make informal collaboration more difficult for some teams.
Which statement accurately describes the relationship?
options: The texts discuss different consequences of remote work, one beneficial and one potentially costly.
Both texts claim remote work has only benefits.
Text 1 discusses transportation policy unrelated to work.
Text 2 says collaboration is impossible in person.
questions.explanation: The authors focus on different trade-offs rather than directly contradicting one another.

questions.text:
Text 1: A paleontologist proposes that a dinosaur species migrated seasonally because fossils occur in two distant regions from similar time periods.
Text 2: Another paleontologist argues that the same fossil pattern could result from two separate resident populations.
How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1?
options: The fossil pattern is compatible with migration but does not uniquely prove it.
The fossils must be from different species.
Seasonal migration is impossible for dinosaurs.
The two regions existed in different geological eras.
questions.explanation: Text 2 provides an alternative explanation for the same evidence, so it would say the evidence is not uniquely diagnostic of migration.

questions.text:
Text 1: Philosopher A argues that anonymity online can protect whistleblowers and political dissidents, making it valuable for public discourse.
Text 2: Philosopher B argues that anonymity can reduce accountability and encourage harmful behavior, but acknowledges that banning it entirely could endanger vulnerable speakers.
Which statement would both authors most likely agree with?
options: Anonymity can have important consequences for who is willing or able to speak online.
Anonymity should be banned in every context.
Anonymous speech is always more truthful than identified speech.
Accountability has no value in public discourse.
questions.explanation: Both texts treat anonymity as consequential for participation, though they emphasize different risks and benefits.

questions.text:
Text 1: A conservation biologist argues that wildlife corridors are valuable because they connect isolated habitats and allow animals to move between them.
Text 2: A landscape ecologist agrees that connectivity matters but cautions that a poorly located corridor can also spread disease or invasive species.
How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1?
options: Connectivity can be beneficial, but corridor design must consider possible ecological costs.
All corridors should be identical in location and width.
questions.explanation: Text 2 accepts the basic benefit but adds conditions and possible costs.

questions.text:
Text 1: A literary critic argues that a novel's unreliable narrator forces readers to question the truth of every event described.
Text 2: Another critic argues that although some factual details are uncertain, the narrator is consistently reliable when describing her own emotions.
Which choice best describes a difference between the critics?
options: Text 1 treats unreliability as broad, while Text 2 limits it to some kinds of information.
Text 1 believes the narrator is emotionally reliable, while Text 2 denies it.
Text 1 discusses poetry, while Text 2 discusses a novel.
Both claim every event is unquestionably accurate.
questions.explanation: The disagreement concerns how far the narrator's unreliability extends.

questions.text:
Text 1: An education researcher reports that students who used retrieval practice scored higher on a later test than students who reread notes.
Text 2: Another researcher points out that the study participants volunteered for an intensive study-skills program and may have been unusually motivated.
How would Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1?
options: The result may be real for the sample, but the participant pool could limit how broadly it can be generalized.
The score difference proves retrieval practice is ineffective.
Volunteer motivation cannot affect study outcomes.
Rereading notes always outperforms retrieval practice.
questions.explanation: Text 2 does not deny the observed result; it questions external validity because of the volunteer sample.

questions.text:
Text 1: A historian argues that the rapid spread of a technology was driven primarily by falling production costs.
Text 2: Another historian shows that costs had already fallen substantially before adoption accelerated and instead emphasizes a later change in regulation.
Which choice best describes the relationship between the texts?
options: Text 2 challenges Text 1's causal explanation by pointing to the timing of cost changes and proposing another factor.
Text 2 agrees that production costs alone explain the timing.
Text 1 and Text 2 discuss unrelated technologies.
Text 2 provides no evidence relevant to Text 1.
questions.explanation: Text 2 uses chronology to weaken the cost-based causal explanation and introduces regulation as an alternative.

questions.text: The new evidence did not completely disprove the earlier theory, but it did _____ several of the theory's strongest claims by showing that they were less certain than previously believed. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
questions.skill: Words in Context - logical and precise
questions.explanation: The evidence makes the claims less strong, so "weaken" is the precise fit.

questions.text: Because the two measurements were taken with different instruments, the researchers were _____ about comparing the values directly. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
questions.skill: Words in Context - tone and logic
questions.explanation: Different instruments create a reason for caution about direct comparison.

questions.text: The success of the restoration project is contingent _____ continued funding for maintenance. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to standard usage?
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "contingent on."

questions.text: The archive remained closed _____ Monday, when staff completed the safety inspection. Which choice completes the text most logically?
questions.skill: Words in Context - preposition of time
questions.explanation: "Until Monday" means up to that point in time.

questions.text: In the sentence "The committee determined the final schedule," the word "determined" most nearly means
questions.skill: Words in Context - meaning in context
questions.explanation: Here "determined" means decided or established, not merely found out.

questions.text: The scientist described the result as _____ rather than conclusive: it pointed toward a possible relationship, but additional experiments would be needed. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
questions.explanation: A suggestive result points in a direction without settling the question.

questions.text: Although the two species look similar, genetic analysis has _____ them as belonging to separate evolutionary lineages. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
questions.skill: Words in Context - logical and precise
questions.explanation: The genetic evidence differentiates the species, so "distinguished" is precise.

questions.text: The policy was designed _____ reducing unnecessary energy use in public buildings. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to standard usage?
questions.explanation: "Designed for" correctly expresses purpose here.

questions.text: The researchers proceeded _____ the assumption that the sensor error was random rather than systematic. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to standard usage?
questions.explanation: The idiomatic expression is "proceed on the assumption."

questions.text: The passage states that a once-popular explanation has "lost currency" among researchers. As used in the passage, "currency" most nearly means
questions.explanation: In this idiom, an idea that has currency is widely accepted or influential.

questions.text: Far from being _____, the two findings can both be true: one describes the average pattern across regions, whereas the other concerns a small subgroup with unusual conditions. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
questions.explanation: The sentence explains why the findings do not contradict each other, so "incompatible" is the word being negated.

questions.text: The historian argues that the treaty was not merely symbolic; it _____ a series of administrative changes that reshaped local government over the next decade. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?
questions.explanation: "Precipitated" means caused or brought about, fitting the changes that followed the treaty.

questions.text: The researchers are careful to distinguish correlation _____ causation, noting that the observational data cannot establish which variable influences the other. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to standard usage?
questions.explanation: The standard expression is "distinguish X from Y."

questions.text: The committee's conclusion rests _____ evidence collected from only two sites, a limitation the report itself acknowledges. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to standard usage?
questions.explanation: The idiomatic phrase is "rests on evidence."

questions.text: A critic writes that the novel "qualifies" its initial optimism by ending with unresolved conflicts. As used in the passage, "qualifies" most nearly means
questions.explanation: Here "qualifies" means modifies or limits a claim, making the optimism less absolute.

questions.text: Two angles of a triangle measure 50 degrees and 60 degrees. What is the measure of the third angle?
questions.explanation: Triangle angles sum to 180 degrees: 180-50-60=70.

questions.text: A right triangle has legs of length 6 and 8. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: 6^2+8^2=36+64=100, so the hypotenuse is 10.

questions.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. What is true about the angles opposite those equal sides?
questions.explanation: Equal sides in an isosceles triangle are opposite equal base angles.

questions.text: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If one corresponding angle measures 112 degrees, what is the measure of the other corresponding angle?
questions.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal when lines are parallel.

questions.text: A triangle has side lengths 5, 7, and 9. Which statement is true?
options: The side lengths can form a triangle.
The side lengths cannot form a triangle because 5+7<9.
questions.explanation: Each pair sums to more than the third side; in particular, 5+7=12>9.

questions.text: In a 30-60-90 triangle, the shortest side has length 7. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: The side ratio is 1:sqrt(3):2, so the hypotenuse is 2(7)=14.

questions.text: In a 45-45-90 triangle, each leg has length 5. What is the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse equals leg times sqrt(2).

questions.text: Two similar triangles have corresponding side lengths 6 and 9 in the smaller triangle and 10 and x in the larger triangle. If 6 corresponds to 10 and 9 corresponds to x, what is x?
questions.explanation: Scale factor is 10/6=5/3, so x=9(5/3)=15.

questions.text: An exterior angle of a triangle measures 125 degrees. One of the two remote interior angles measures 48 degrees. What is the other remote interior angle?
questions.explanation: Exterior angle=two remote interior angles: 125=48+x, so x=77.

questions.text: Lines l and m are parallel. A transversal creates two same-side interior angles measuring (3x+10) degrees and (5x+26) degrees. What is x?
questions.explanation: Same-side interior angles are supplementary: 3x+10+5x+26=180, so 8x=144 and x=18.

questions.text: An isosceles triangle has equal sides of length 13 and base length 10. What is its area?
questions.explanation: The altitude bisects the base into 5 and 5. Height=sqrt(13^2-5^2)=12. Area=(1/2)(10)(12)=60.

questions.text: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF. AB=8, BC=12, AC=14, and DE=20 corresponds to AB. What is the perimeter of triangle DEF?
questions.explanation: Scale factor=20/8=2.5. Original perimeter=34, so new perimeter=34(2.5)=85.

questions.text: A right triangle has hypotenuse 17 and one leg 8. What is the length of the other leg?
questions.explanation: Other leg=sqrt(17^2-8^2)=sqrt(289-64)=sqrt225=15.

questions.text: Two sides of a triangle have lengths 11 and 17. Which value could be the length of the third side?
questions.explanation: The third side x must satisfy |17-11|<x<28, so 6<x<28. Only 12 works.

questions.text: In triangle ABC, angle A=40 degrees and angle B=65 degrees. A second triangle DEF has angle D=40 degrees and angle E=65 degrees. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: Two pairs of equal angles are enough for similarity (AA), but not for congruence or equal size.
